## 321197: group versus group-list edge colourings
Actual 1102.4980v3 pp1–4 was read, including all group definitions, Theorems1.1–1.3, Conjectures1.4/1.5, Lemma2.1 proof, and the explanation of the cycle obstruction. Finite simple undirected graphs and Abelian groups are standing hypotheses. Equality is source Conjecture1.5, not a proved conclusion of the following restricted planar results. The corpus resolved annotation has no paid bridge.

Route A, greedy extension and minimal counterexamples. In the line graph an edge uv of G conflicts with d(u)+d(v)-2 previously coloured edges. For each such neighbour, its assigned colour and the fixed edge gain forbid at most one group element at the new vertex; either orientation simply changes the sign. Thus a list of size q extends whenever d(u)+d(v)-2<q. This works for arbitrary Abelian group size at least q and arbitrary lists, with no probabilistic assumption. A fixed-instance minimal obstruction to q-choosability consequently has every remaining edge degree sum at least q+2. This proves a usable structural reduction but does not compare q to the group chromatic number of G in general. To obtain equality one must rule out all such critical line graphs at q=chi'_g(G); the sum inequality alone does not do this.

Route B, cycles and the failure of the standard repair. Orient a cycle consistently over Z/2 and set lists={0,1}. Each forbidden gain condition forces the complementary difference: c_i-c_(i+1)=1-f_i in Z/2. Summing around the cycle requires sum_i(1-f_i)=0. Choose the f_i so this sum is 1; no colouring exists. Therefore two available colours on each edge of a residual even cycle do not suffice in the group model. Ordinary even-cycle list-edge-colouring cannot close the induction. This explains the actual source warning by an explicit all-length ordinary argument, not an executed search. It supplies no counterexample to the conjectured equality: the same gains obstruct the corresponding two-colour group colouring too. With three colours a cycle can be coloured by greedy path extension and the final vertex avoiding at most two forbidden values. Thus the cycle gives equal parameters, not a gap.

Route C, larger-group encoding. A tempting reduction takes an arbitrary q-list assignment in A and embeds it in a larger Abelian group B so that a B-group-colouring lands in the chosen lists. But the definition of group chromatic number permits the entire B as palette, and pairwise difference restrictions do not force vertex-specific membership without adding constraint vertices or edges. Such additions generally leave the given line graph and change its group chromatic number. A construction of membership gadgets preserving line-graph realizability and the exact q threshold is absent. No claim of universal equality, explicit gap witness, or current public resolution survives. Greedy subcases and cycles are not credited helpers.

## 317859: Seidel deck reconstruction
Actual 0810.3189 definitions2.1–2.3, Theorem2.6/Corollary2.8 context, Section5 definitions and Conjecture2, and Section7.1 were read as text. Material counterexample diagrams were not visually audited and are not used as certificates. The source distinguishes its own norm/cospectral examples by their decks. Stanley's vertex-switching reconstruction and digraph switching decks found by search are different questions: they do not refute this one.

Route A, two-graph parity. For each vertex triple define t(abc) in F2 as the sum of its three adjacency indicators. A switch on any set toggles zero or two edges in each triple, so t is invariant. Conversely if two labelled graphs have the same t, let d_ab be their edgewise difference. Fix r and put s_r=0, s_a=d_ra. Triple parity at r,a,b gives d_ab=s_a+s_b, so switching by s converts one graph into the other. Thus full labelled triangle parity is a complete switching invariant; after relabelling it is complete for switching equivalence. This is an ordinary fully proved bridge. The deck only provides the unlabelled restrictions of this parity structure. The missing statement is a compatible gluing of all card relabellings, not invariance of t.

At n4, the four triple parities sum to zero because each edge is counted twice. Their support therefore has size0,2,or4. S4 acts transitively on subsets of each such size (triples are indexed by their omitted vertices). Each three-vertex switching class records exactly its triple parity, so the deck determines that support size and hence the whole switching class at n4. This is one endpoint/subcase, not a solution for all n>=4 and receives no credit.

Route B, lower substructure counts. For any fixed two-graph pattern T on s<n vertices, each induced T-subset of an n-vertex object appears in precisely n-s cards. Summing its occurrences over the deck and dividing by n-s reconstructs its count. This pays all proper induced pattern counts, but does not prove that those counts separate n-vertex two-graphs. Such a separation theorem would itself solve the reconstruction target. A mere inventory of traces or triangle counts loses the necessary incidence information.

Route C, Seidel characteristic polynomials. Switching and relabelling conjugate the Seidel matrix by signed permutations. Thus equal switching decks give equal multisets of principal (n-1)-submatrix characteristic polynomials. The derivative of det(tI-S) is their sum: multilinearity of determinant differentiates one diagonal t at a time. Hence the two full monic characteristic polynomials have equal derivative and can differ by a constant only. There is no paid deduction of that constant or of switching equivalence even if spectra agree; source Section4/7 expressly describes distinct cospectral switching classes. The attempted spectral shortcut fails at two separate bridges. Normalizing one root to be isolated likewise gives a representative graph, but independent normalizations of deleted cards do not provide globally compatible root choices. No exact full-scope pair or reconstruction proof was obtained.
